Where to pay your Philadelphia property tax

Billing and collection of the Real Estate Tax belong to the Department of Revenue, and the Office of Property Assessment supplies the value the bill rests on. You pay once a year. One March 31 due date covers both the City and the School District.

  • Online: the Philadelphia Tax Center, using the property address or the OPA account number. An eCheck carries no processing charge, while debit and credit cards do.
  • By phone: (833) 913-0795.
  • By mail: check or money order payable to the City of Philadelphia, sent with the OPA account number to Department of Revenue, PO Box 8409, Philadelphia, PA 19101-8409.
  • In person: the Municipal Services Building at 1401 John F. Kennedy Blvd. takes cash. Satellite offices at 7522 Castor Ave. and 2761 N. 22nd St. take no cash. Offices open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

The rate for tax year 2025 is 1.3998 percent of assessed value.

What happens when a bill goes unpaid?

The account moves through a fixed ladder. Charges begin the day after the March 31 deadline and grow until the City treats the balance as delinquent and can move toward foreclosure.

  • From April 1: additions of 1.5 percent a month, running to January 1.
  • January 1: a further addition of up to 15 percent, a lien in the amount of the whole delinquency, and the account is registered delinquent.
  • February 1: penalties, attorney's fees and other costs are layered on.
  • Any time after that: legal action, which can end in a sheriff sale of the house at public auction.

The Department sends a Warning of Risk of Tax Foreclosure to accounts with a balance and no payment agreement. A current-year bill left unpaid through the end of the year lets the City start foreclosure, and debt from earlier years can be pursued at any time. The notice also points owners to free housing counseling and legal help through the City's housing agencies.

Owner-occupied Payment Agreement

The Owner-occupied Payment Agreement, or OOPA, lets a homeowner who lives in the house repay old tax in monthly amounts tied to income. An owner whose name is not on the deed can qualify if a legal interest in the home can be shown, and no down payment is needed. Some low-income and senior households pay $0 a month.

OOPA tiers, shown for a one-person household

Tiers 4 and 5 fold new year taxes into the agreement. Everyone else must pay each new March 31 bill in full on top of the monthly plan amount. Applicants show two forms of proof of residence, one a government photo ID, and income records such as tax returns, pay stubs or benefit letters. In tier 3, half the accrued interest is waived. A review of actual expenses is available when the tiered amount is unaffordable.

Other City charges that can become liens

Property tax is not the only debt that can attach to the parcel. The City can also file liens for several other charges:

  • Water and sewer charges, with questions going to the Water Revenue Bureau at (215) 685-6300.
  • Commercial trash fees, previously called refuse fees.
  • Department of Licenses and Inspections abatement invoices.
  • Nuisance and demolition fees and fines.

Water liens can be searched at water-lien.phila.gov, which reports up to 15 years of recorded liens. A search there does not replace a title search, and it may omit court costs. If it shows a lien, a payoff request form goes to the Water Department by email.

Relief programs for homeowners

The City runs several programs that cut a bill or spread it out, and the Tax Center has a combined application that checks eligibility for five of them at once. Owners already enrolled generally do not reapply unless the property changes hands.

  • The Homestead Exemption takes $100,000 off the taxable assessment of an owner-occupied home in 2027, and most owners save about $1,399.
  • The Real Estate Tax installment plan lets seniors and income-qualified owners pay the year in monthly installments instead of one lump sum.
  • The senior and low-income freezes hold the tax at its current level even if rates or values climb.
  • The Longtime Owner Occupants Program caps the taxable value for owners of ten or more years whose assessment jumped 50 percent in a year or 75 percent over five.
  • A credit applies to the City portion for reserve and National Guard members called to active duty.

Pennsylvania's own Property Tax/Rent Rebate program for seniors and adults with disabilities does not require a City tax receipt.

Selling a Philadelphia house when tax is due

Tax debt does not block a sale. The closing figure simply has to cover what the City is owed.

  1. Look up the balance on the Philadelphia Tax Center by address or OPA number.
  2. Search water-lien.phila.gov and send a water payoff form at least 30 days before settlement.
  3. Ask a housing counselor about an OOPA first if you want to stay in the home.
  4. Order a title search to catch trash fee, abatement and other liens.
  5. Budget for the 4.578 percent realty transfer tax and the deed recording fee.

A seller on a short clock can ask for a cash offer, and the title company settles the City's claim at the table. That route also skips repairs, listing prep and showings, which matters when a delinquent account is already moving toward the January 1 lien.

Local housing context

Philadelphia has a July 2025 population estimate of 1,574,281. A typical owned home is valued at $243,100, and 51.8 percent of households own, so renters make up nearly half. Median gross rent is $1,397 a month and median household income is $61,953. Neighborhood prices vary widely, so a countywide figure is only a rough guide for any one house.

What to have ready before a tax-related sale

Documents save time at the closing table. Gather the OPA account number, the latest tax bill and any Warning of Risk of Tax Foreclosure letter, and keep a copy of any signed payment agreement. Bring the water payoff response if a lien turned up. If you live in the house, tell the title company about your Homestead Exemption and any freeze, because the balance on file can differ from what you expect. If an agreement is active, ask the Department of Revenue how it is treated when the house sells, so the figure at settlement is not a surprise.

Keep paying the current bill while the sale is pending. Additions of 1.5 percent a month do not pause because a contract is signed, and a lien filed on January 1 would have to be paid from the proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

Who do I call about a Philadelphia property tax balance?

The Department of Revenue. You can check a balance on the Philadelphia Tax Center or call (833) 913-0795. Water charges go to the Water Revenue Bureau at (215) 685-6300.

What if I cannot pay in full?

Apply for a payment agreement. An owner who lives in the house can ask for an OOPA, and owners who do not live there can request a standard agreement. Income-based programs can lower or pause payments.

Can Philadelphia take my house for unpaid property tax?

Yes, after the account becomes delinquent and a lien is filed. The City can then seek a court order to sell the house at a sheriff sale. A signed payment agreement or full payment stops the process.

Do penalties start on March 31?

They start April 1. Additions of 1.5 percent a month accrue from that date until January 1, when the larger delinquency charges apply.

Does the buyer or seller pay the tax at closing?

The seller covers what is owed through closing, taken from the seller's side of the settlement statement. The 4.578 percent transfer tax is normally split, though the City may collect it from either party.

Who handles property tax in Pittsburgh

Pittsburgh owners deal with three taxing bodies: the city, the school district and Allegheny County. The city's Real Estate Division bills and collects the city tax, while the county sets the assessed value that every rate is applied to. The tax applies to all owners of real estate within the city and school district, and it is the millage rate multiplied by the assessed value.

The Real Estate Division sits at 414 Grant Street and answers at 412-255-2525. Chapter 263 of the Pittsburgh Code covers the tax. Bills usually go out in the middle of January, with installment bills mailed in April and July.

The county's role is separate. The Allegheny County Office of Property Assessments decides what your house is worth for tax purposes, and the Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review hears disputes. If your bill looks wrong, work out whether the problem is the value (a county matter) or the payment record (a city matter) before you call anyone.

Due dates and discount

The year's bill can be paid in one amount or in three installments, and the dates repeat every year.

  • February 10: last day to take the 2 percent discount, on either the full annual amount or the first installment
  • February 27: first installment due, or the annual amount at its gross figure
  • April 30: second installment due
  • July 31: third installment due

The first installment is where people get caught. A payment that misses the end of February, or falls short of the whole first installment, makes the entire year's tax due, with interest running from March 1. An online payment portal run by Magic Collection Solutions is linked from the city's tax page.

A taxpayer who misses the discount can ask for an extension using the discount extension form on the city's Real Estate Forms page.

Pittsburgh millage rates

Three rates stack on a Pittsburgh bill. For 2026 they are 6.43 mills for the county, 9.67 for the city and 10.457 for the school district, a combined 26.557 mills. In 2025 the city rate was 8.06 and the county rate was 6.43, and in 2024 the county rate was 4.73. The taxable residential median value is $68,600.

How to appeal your assessment

Value disputes go to the Allegheny County Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review, which sits outside city government. The board now handles scheduling and hearing notices on its own.

Annual appeals are filed in a summer window. The most recent one ran from July 1 to September 1. A person who misses it may file under limited circumstances, but first has to submit a late-filed appeal form. Call the county before the next window opens.

  • Residential hearing notices are mailed at least 14 days ahead; commercial notices at least 21 days ahead.
  • The board meets every two weeks at 8:00 am in Room 328 of the County Office Building, 542 Forbes Avenue.
  • The 2027 common level ratio is 49.3 percent, and it applies to current market value in appeals heard starting September 2026.

An appeal compares the assessed value with market value after that ratio is applied. Bring recent comparable sales and any repair estimates to the hearing.

Homestead and senior relief

Two measures are meant to lower a city bill: the Act 50 homestead exemption of $15,000 and the Act 77 senior tax relief, a 40 percent reduction on assessment.

Eligibility rules, forms and filing dates come from the county and city offices, so ask the Real Estate Division or the Office of Property Assessments before you assume a reduction applies to your parcel.

Selling a Pittsburgh house with back taxes

Old delinquent taxes are split between two collectors. The city keeps prior-year delinquent City, Library and Parks real estate taxes and answers questions at 412-255-2525. Prior-year delinquent school taxes were turned over to Jordan Tax Service, Inc., which takes payment arrangements at 412-345-7960.

The city's delinquency list can be downloaded by anyone, but it may not show the current owner if the county has not yet reported a transfer, may not reflect assessment changes decided on appeal, and may leave out accounts under $50. A title search is the safer check, and the payoff figure should come directly from the city and the collection agency in writing.

At settlement, the agent subtracts unpaid taxes from what the seller receives and sends the money to the collectors. If the debts exceed the price, the settlement statement shows the shortfall before anyone signs.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What does the transfer tax cost on a Pittsburgh sale?

Allegheny County realty transfer tax runs from 2 to 5 percent, and Pittsburgh sits at the top of that range. For a house in the city the total is 5 percent: 1 percent to the state, 3 percent to the city and 1 percent to the Pittsburgh School District. The city applied the 5 percent rate to residential deeds recorded starting February 1, 2020.

Payment happens at recording, on its own check apart from the recording fees. Both sides are liable under state rules, and certain transfers, such as inheritances, are exempt. The sale contract decides who actually pays.

Pittsburgh housing at a glance

Pittsburgh covers about 55 square miles in the center of Allegheny County, with steep slopes and floodplains along the Allegheny, Monongahela and Ohio rivers. Slope and flood exposure differ a great deal from one neighborhood to the next, which can affect price and insurance. The mid 2025 population is 307,632. Owners occupy 47.7 percent of occupied homes, so renters make up the majority of households. An owned home typically carries a $205,800 value, and median household income is $65,742.

Getting ready to sell

A short list covers most of what a Pittsburgh seller needs.

  1. Gather the latest city and school bills and note whether you paid by installment or in full.
  2. Call the Real Estate Division at 412-255-2525 for a balance, and ask Jordan Tax Service, Inc. at 412-345-7960 about any prior-year school taxes.
  3. Add up the 5 percent transfer tax and decide how the contract splits it.
  4. Have a recent comparable sales list on hand in case the buyer asks why the assessment looks high or low.

A cash sale skips the listing and repair steps, but the tax payoff and transfer tax work the same way at the closing table.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Pittsburgh discount deadline?

February 10. Paying the full annual tax or the first installment by that date earns a 2 percent discount. After that, the gross amount is due February 27.

What happens if I skip the first installment?

You owe the whole year at once, and interest starts March 1. The same result follows from paying less than the full first installment.

Where can I get answers on a Pittsburgh tax bill?

Call the city's Real Estate Division at 412-255-2525 or visit 414 Grant Street. Questions about the value itself belong with the Allegheny County Office of Property Assessments.

When can I appeal my Pittsburgh assessment?

Annual appeals are filed in a summer window, July 1 to September 1 in the most recent cycle. A late-filed appeal form is available under limited circumstances. Ask the county for the next window.

Who gets paid when a house with back taxes sells?

The title company pays them from the seller's proceeds. Delinquent city taxes go to the city, and prior-year school taxes go to Jordan Tax Service, Inc. Get written payoff figures first.
